content: The California School for the Blind is a public educational institution serving blind children from kindergarten through 12th grade. It is located in Fremont, California, adjacent to the California School for the Deaf. The education of blind children in the San Francisco area began in 1860 with the establishment of the Society for the Instruction and Maintenance of the Indigent Deaf and Dumb, and the Blind in California. This initiative was led by Mrs. Frances Clark, who served as the school’s first principal until 1865. In 1865, Dr. Warring Wilkinson joined the school and initiated efforts to transition it into a state-supported institution. Under his leadership, the school, then known as the California State Asylum for the Deaf, Dumb, and Blind, relocated to what would later become Berkeley in 1867. In 1906, an amendment to the Political Code renamed the school the California Institution for the Deaf and Blind and formally integrated it into the California State school system. Dr. Wilkinson retired in 1910. In 1914, the Legislature replaced the term Institution with School, renaming it the California School for the Deaf and Blind. In 1922, the school was legislatively divided into two separate programs: the California School for the Blind (CSB) and the California School for the Deaf. However, the formal separation, marked by the completion of a new classroom building, did not occur until July 1929. In 1943, the California School for the Blind received authorization from the state legislature to admit deaf-blind students, becoming the third school in the United States to establish a program for this population. The first deaf-blind student graduated from CSB in 1949. The school’s enrollment peaked in 1965 with 167 students. By 1973, the California Department of Education determined that the school needed to relocate to a site better suited for accessibility and compliance with updated earthquake and fire safety standards. A new campus was constructed in Fremont, California, and the school moved to its current location in 1980. The original Berkeley campus, established in 1867, featured a Victorian Gothic stone building that was destroyed by fire in January 1875. Temporary buildings were used for classes until new facilities were constructed, including an educational building, dormitories, support facilities, and a principal’s residence. In 1890, a Spanish Colonial Revival educational building was completed, featuring an assembly hall and a 160-foot tower with a Seth Thomas clock. This building survived the 1906 San Francisco earthquake with minor damage. Over the years, additional buildings were added, including a gymnasium in 1915, dormitories in 1925 and 1929, and the Helen Keller Building for deaf-blind classes in 1949. Helen Keller attended the dedication of the building named in her honor. In the 1970s, the school began its transition to the Fremont site, completing the move in 1980. The Berkeley campus was designated a Berkeley Landmark in 1981 and added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1982. The former site was divided between the University of California and the city of Berkeley, with the university establishing the Clark Kerr Campus residential complex and the city creating Redwood Gardens, a housing facility for financially needy elderly individuals. The California School for the Blind follows a nationally accepted expanded core curriculum tailored for students who are blind or visually impaired. This curriculum includes training in Braille reading and writing, orientation and mobility, assistive technology, career education, adapted physical education, music, art, recreation and leisure, independent living skills, and functional academics. Extracurricular activities at the school are diverse and include swimming, karate, goalball, tandem bicycling, music groups, dance groups, international pen pals on tape, art, cooking, and roller skating. Many of the school’s athletes participate in the Alameda County Special Olympics team and the United States Association of Blind Athletes.
